solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 swaps the roles of Articles 198 and 199. Students who know 'Article 198 relates to state Money Bills' without distinguishing procedure (198) from definition (199) will accept Statement 3. The article numbers are adjacent and the functions are closely related — a classic entity-swap within a narrow numerical range that UPSC exploits repeatedly.
solution.final_explanation:

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 207 at the state level mirrors Article 117 at the central level, providing the equivalent of FB-1 and FB-2 frameworks for state legislatures.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The FB-1 vs FB-2 distinction is designed around the existence of a second chamber. In unicameral state legislatures (which constitute the majority of Indian states), there is no Vidhan Parishad to exercise differential powers — rendering the procedural distinction practically irrelevant.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Article 198 mirrors Article 109 — it deals with the procedure for passing Money Bills in state legislatures (restrictions on Vidhan Parishad's role). The definition of Money Bills for state legislatures is in Article 199, which mirrors Article 110. The statement reverses 198 and 199's roles.

Value Addition:

• Article 199's definition of state Money Bills mirrors Article 110(1)'s seven-matter list but adapted for state finance.
• For states without a Vidhan Parishad, all bills pass through the Vidhan Sabha alone, making the upper-house differential treatment provisions redundant.

solution.concept_anchor: 14-day limit applies to FB-1 but no equivalent time limit for FB-2

statement_analysis.statement: The Constitution prescribes a 14-day time limit within which the Rajya Sabha must act on a Financial Bill (Category 1); failure to do so results in the bill being deemed passed by both Houses.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 109(5) applies to FB-1 through its Money Bill procedural alignment — if Rajya Sabha does not pass, reject or return FB-1 within 14 days of receiving it, the bill is deemed passed by both Houses.

statement_analysis.statement: Similarly, the Constitution prescribes a 14-day time limit for the Rajya Sabha to act on a Financial Bill (Category 2); if no action is taken within this period, the bill is deemed passed.
statement_analysis.reason: FB-2 follows Ordinary Bill procedure — there is no 14-day limit or deemed-passed clause for FB-2. Rajya Sabha's inaction on an Ordinary Bill creates a 6-month deadlock condition that can trigger a joint sitting under Article 108, not automatic passage.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (both correct) is the strong distractor because Statement 1 is clearly correct, and students who know '14 days applies to financial bills' may extend it to FB-2 without carefully checking which bill type is covered by the deemed-passed clause.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1 — FB-1 follows Money Bill procedure including the 14-day limit and deemed-passed clause. Correct.
Test Statement 2 — FB-2 follows Ordinary Bill procedure; no 14-day limit or deemed-passed clause applies; the 6-month deadlock + joint sitting mechanism applies instead.
Statement 1 is correct; Statement 2 is incorrect — answer is option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 extends the 14-day / deemed-passed rule to FB-2 by using the word 'similarly' — suggesting parallel treatment. This scope-extension from FB-1 to FB-2 is the exact trap UPSC exploits in single-liner assertion questions. The 14-day / deemed-passed mechanism is the sharpest differentiator between FB-1 (Money Bill procedure) and FB-2 (Ordinary Bill procedure). Students who conflate 'Financial Bills' as a unified category will accept Statement 2.
solution.final_explanation:
The 14-day rule and deemed-passed clause are among the most precise one-liners that separate FB-1 from FB-2 in UPSC questions.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 109(5) creates a 14-day window for Rajya Sabha on Money Bills. Since FB-1 follows Money Bill procedure, this window applies equally to FB-1. If Rajya Sabha neither acts nor returns the bill within 14 days, it is deemed passed by both Houses — a constitutional override of Rajya Sabha inaction.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The word 'similarly' in the statement is the trap. FB-2 follows Ordinary Bill procedure — it has no 14-day limit and no deemed-passed clause. Rajya Sabha can hold an FB-2 indefinitely (subject only to the 6-month deadlock provision), after which a joint sitting may be convened. Automatic passage without Rajya Sabha action is not available for FB-2.

Value Addition:
• The 6-month deadlock condition for Ordinary Bills and FB-2: if Rajya Sabha rejects the bill, passes it with unacceptable amendments, or fails to pass it within 6 months, a joint sitting can be called.
• The deemed-passed mechanism works in Lok Sabha's favour — it means Rajya Sabha's silence or delay cannot block financial legislation classified as FB-1.
• For Ordinary Bills, unlike FB-1, no 'deemed passed' outcome is possible — only joint sitting resolution.

solution.concept_anchor: Bill involving audit of CFI accounts — Article 110(1)(g) as Money Bill trigger
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (FB-2) is the strong distractor because the bill involves CFI — a clear FB-2 trigger for students who know 'CFI = FB-2' without checking whether the bill also contains an Article 110 matter (audit of CFI accounts is clause (g) of Article 110(1)).

Apply the classification test: bill contains only Article 110 matters (audit clause) → Money Bill.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap exploits incomplete recall of the seven Article 110 matters. Most students remember taxation, borrowing, and appropriation as Article 110 matters — but audit of government accounts (clause (g)) is less frequently recalled. A student who sees 'CFI accounts' and 'audit' will think 'financial + CFI = FB-2', missing the fact that audit of CFI accounts is itself an Article 110(1)(g) matter. This turns what looks like an FB-2 scenario into a Money Bill scenario.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 110(1) lists seven matters that define a Money Bill. Clause (g) specifically includes the custody, issue, or audit of the accounts of the Union or a State. A bill dealing exclusively with the procedure for auditing accounts of the Consolidated Fund of India falls squarely within this clause.

• Option (a): Correct — since the bill contains only Article 110(1)(g) matter (audit of CFI accounts) and no other provisions, it is a Money Bill. The Speaker will certify it under Article 110(3).
• Option (b): Incorrect — FB-2 applies to bills involving CFI expenditure but containing no Article 110 matter. Since audit of CFI accounts is itself an Article 110(1)(g) matter, FB-2 classification is unavailable.
• Option (c): Incorrect — FB-1 requires Article 110 matters plus other provisions. Since this bill contains only Article 110 content, it is a pure Money Bill, not an FB-1.
• Option (d): Incorrect — an Ordinary Bill has neither Article 110 content nor CFI expenditure triggers; this bill has Article 110 content.

Value Addition:

• Article 148 establishes the CAG; Article 149 defines CAG's duties — legislation under Article 149 may be a Money Bill.

solution.concept_anchor: Speaker certification exclusive to Money Bills — FB-1 and FB-2 have no certification

statement_analysis.statement: Since a Financial Bill (Category 1) is introduced in the Lok Sabha with Presidential recommendation — just as a Money Bill is — the Speaker of the Lok Sabha must certify it as a Financial Bill before transmitting it to the Rajya Sabha.
statement_analysis.reason: Speaker certification under Article 110(3) applies exclusively to Money Bills. No certification is required or available for FB-1, even though it shares the Lok Sabha introduction and Presidential recommendation features with Money Bills.

statement_analysis.statement: The Speaker's certification of a bill as a Money Bill is open to judicial review if a citizen can demonstrate that the bill contained provisions not falling under Article 110(1).
statement_analysis.reason: Article 110(3) explicitly makes the Speaker's certification final; it cannot be questioned in any court of law. The Aadhaar case majority upheld this non-justiciability, even when critics argued the certified bill contained non-Article 110 provisions.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (1 only NOT correct) is the strong distractor because students who correctly identify Statement 1 as wrong may then hesitate on Statement 2, not recalling that Article 110(3) shields the certification from judicial review — especially in the wake of the Aadhaar case, where the Court did examine the issue.
elimination_logic: Test Statement 1 — Speaker certification is exclusive to Money Bills; FB-1 gets no certificate despite sharing other features. Statement 1 is NOT correct.

Test Statement 2 — Article 110(3) makes Speaker certification final and non-justiciable; the Aadhaar case majority upheld this; courts cannot review it even with evidence of non-Article 110 content. Statement 2 is NOT correct.
Both statements are NOT correct — the answer is option b (1 and 2 both NOT correct), mapped to the option pattern: (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2.

Wait — re-check: the options for a 2-statement NOT correct question follow pattern: (a) 1 only NOT correct, (b) 2 only NOT correct, (c) Both NOT correct, (d) Neither is NOT correct (i.e., both are correct). Since both statements are NOT correct, answer is c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the Aadhaar case's ambiguity. Students who know the Supreme Court 'examined' the Money Bill certification in Aadhaar may conclude that judicial review IS possible, making Statement 2 look correct. But the Court's majority explicitly upheld the non-justiciability principle of Article 110(3) — the fact that the Court examined the question at all is a procedural anomaly, not a reversal of Article 110(3)'s protection. The minority's critique was dissent, not law.
solution.final_explanation:
Both statements in this question are incorrect — the question tests two of the most commonly misunderstood aspects of Speaker certification.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Speaker certification under Article 110(3) is reserved exclusively for Money Bills. FB-1 travels to Rajya Sabha without any Speaker's certificate — despite sharing Lok Sabha-only introduction and Presidential recommendation with Money Bills. This distinction is constitutionally significant: Money Bills are shielded by non-justiciability; FB-1 is not.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 110(3) makes the Speaker's certificate final and non-justiciable. No court can question it, even with evidence that the bill contained non-Article 110 provisions. In the Aadhaar case (2018), the Supreme Court majority upheld this position — the Court engaged with the substance but ultimately found that the non-justiciability principle holds. The minority's view calling it 'fraud on the Constitution' was dissent, not binding law.

Both statements are NOT correct — answer is option c.

Value Addition:
• The non-justiciability of Speaker's certification creates what scholars call a 'constitutional gap' — there is no check on a Speaker who incorrectly certifies a bill as a Money Bill.
• Rajya Sabha has no procedural mechanism to challenge a Money Bill certificate — it must act as though the bill is a Money Bill.
• The minority opinion in the Aadhaar case remains the most powerful academic challenge to the non-justiciability principle.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option b targets students who confuse the stage of Presidential recommendation across bill types. solution.final_explanation:
Presidential recommendation is a constitutional prerequisite for certain categories of bills — but it does not apply to all legislation. The question tests which bill type requires no Presidential recommendation at any stage.

• Option (a): Incorrect — 'before introduction' is the requirement for Money Bills and FB-1, not a universal requirement. Ordinary Bills never require this.

• Option (c): Incorrect — India's Constitution does not require Presidential recommendation 'before Royal Assent' for any bill. Assent is the President's final act of approval under Articles 111 or 109, not a stage requiring prior recommendation.

• Presidential recommendation under Article 117 is distinct from Presidential assent under Article 111 — they occur at different stages and serve different constitutional functions.
• Recommendation is a precondition for introduction/consideration; assent is the final step after both Houses pass the bill.
• The President can withhold assent (return a bill) for Ordinary Bills — but cannot withhold assent from Money Bills under Article 111.

Understanding why requires connecting two facts: (1) FB-2 follows Ordinary Bill procedure, and (2) the deemed-passed clause is a feature of Money Bill procedure, not Ordinary Bill procedure.

• Assertion (A): Correct — FB-2 has no deemed-passed clause. If Rajya Sabha neither passes nor returns an FB-2 within any time frame, the bill does not automatically become law. The deadlock must be resolved through Article 108 joint sitting.
• Reason (R): Correct — FB-2 is treated as an Ordinary Bill in all procedural respects beyond Presidential recommendation. Joint sitting under Article 108 is the Ordinary Bill's deadlock resolution mechanism, and FB-2 inherits this.
• Causal link: R explains A directly. FB-2 has no deemed-passed clause because it follows Ordinary Bill procedure — which has no such clause. The joint sitting route is the replacement mechanism for FB-2's deadlock resolution. R is the constitutionally correct explanation for A.

Correct option is a.

Value Addition:
• The deemed-passed clause effectively eliminates Rajya Sabha's veto power on Money Bills and FB-1 — turning any RS inaction into a Lok Sabha victory.
• For FB-2, Rajya Sabha retains genuine veto power — it can reject the bill and force a joint sitting where Lok Sabha's larger numbers may prevail, but the process is formal.
• The design distinction reflects the Constitution's calibrated approach: fiscal sovereignty of Lok Sabha on taxation/appropriation (FB-1 / Money Bill) but bicameral equality on other financial matters (FB-2).

solution.final_explanation:
Budget-cycle legislation in India involves several different bill types, each requiring correct classification for proper parliamentary treatment.

• Option (a): Incorrectly matched — the Finance Bill (presented with Union Budget) is a Money Bill, not a Financial Bill (Category 1). The Speaker certifies it under Article 110(3).
• Option (b): Incorrectly matched — a Supplementary Appropriation Bill provides additional authorisation to withdraw from CFI (appropriation = Article 110(1)(d) matter). It is therefore a Money Bill, not FB-2.
• Option (c): Correctly matched — a Vote on Account is a temporary authorisation allowing the government to withdraw from CFI before the full Budget is passed. Since it involves appropriation from CFI (Article 110(1)(d)), it is classified as a Money Bill, introduced in Lok Sabha with Presidential recommendation and Speaker's certificate.
• Option (d): Incorrectly matched — a bill establishing a public sector enterprise with CFI funding involves CFI expenditure but no Article 110 matter (the enterprise's governance structure is not an Article 110 provision). Such a bill is FB-2, not a Money Bill.

Value Addition:
• Vote on Account is typically for two months' expenditure at one-sixth of the budgeted amount.
• It is presented immediately after the Budget presentation and passed before April 1 (start of new financial year).
• The Demands for Grants for Vote on Account are passed without detailed discussion — unlike the full Budget.
